topics.topic: Algorithm for classifying stat-family paths under the runtime, including normalization, dir_fd, symlinks, and scandir entries
questions: How is “under” decided for relative paths and paths containing `.`, `..`, repeated separators, bytes, or `PathLike` values; in particular, are dot segments normalized before the runtime-boundary check?
What happens when a path lexically below the runtime is a symbolic link to a changing file outside it?
What exact lexical operation determines whether a stat-family path is under the runtime, especially when the supplied path is relative or is interpreted relative to dir_fd?
What exact lexical or descriptor-relative algorithm decides whether a stat-family path is under the read-only runtime?

Must every `DirEntry.stat()` result be masked according to the path passed to `scandir`, the entry's constructed path, its underlying descriptor, or some other rule, and does the answer change with `follow_symlinks`?

quotes:
A file's
   timestamps read through `os.stat`, `os.lstat`, `os.fstat`, `os.scandir` and their
   `posix` namesakes are zero for a descriptor and for every path not under the
   read-only runtime, judged on the path as the code gives it, without resolving a
   link; a file of the runtime keeps the timestamps its release installed, which
   are no clock because they never change.
judgement.divergence: One implementation classifies the literal supplied pathname lexically, while another normalizes dot segments or incorporates `dir_fd`; the run caller or trial reader observes a retained runtime timestamp versus zero.
judgement.why: The rule defines neither the lexical normalization nor descriptor-relative treatment used to decide whether a supplied path is under the runtime.

witness.initial: The sandbox has its read-only runtime at `/usr`, its exchange directory at `/exchange`, and the implementation has created `/exchange/x` with a nonzero timestamp.
events: The agent runs an implementation that calls `os.stat('/usr/../exchange/x')` and returns its modification timestamp.
outcomes: A literal-prefix classification treats the supplied spelling as under `/usr` and preserves the nonzero timestamp.
A dot-normalized classification treats the effective path as `/exchange/x` and returns zero.
witness.observer: The agent or owner receiving the function output and its digest.
basis:
Every function execution, in trial and in a run alike, runs in a fresh
   isolated environment created by the sandbox: Linux `bubblewrap` with new user,
   PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces, no network interface but the namespace's own loopback — up, as bubblewrap leaves it in a new network namespace, and reaching nothing outside the execution, so K-02's "no network" holds; this is a property of how the kernel starts bubblewrap, which the kernel does not inspect or verify at run time — the start check (rule 8) asks only that a probe execution succeeds — an environment
   holding only `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` (rule 2), a read-only runtime, and one private exchange directory in which every file the code writes is
   bounded by `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` (rule 5).

An implementation is a Python module that defines a top-level function `run`
   taking one argument, a dict with one entry per input port, and returning a dict
   with exactly one entry per output port.

A file's
   timestamps read through `os.stat`, `os.lstat`, `os.fstat`, `os.scandir` and their
   `posix` namesakes are zero for a descriptor and for every path not under the
   read-only runtime, judged on the path as the code gives it, without resolving a
   link; a file of the runtime keeps the timestamps its release installed, which
   are no clock because they never change.

topics.topic: Module names and name-matching rules covered by the fresh-import trap
questions: Exactly which module names are covered: every module named anywhere in rule 4’s full replacement list, or only the modules named by the newly added entry points?
Does the fresh-import rule cover every module named anywhere in rule 4's complete replacement list, or only modules named in the newly appended list beginning with time.clock_gettime?
Exactly which module names cause a fresh import to record a trap hit, and are names matched exactly or by package/submodule relationship?

quotes: runner_source: [BEHAVIOR] The program MUST, before it loads the code, import every module its lists name and only then replace every entry point named in raise_on_call with one that raises whatever arguments it is called with, those in raise_without_argument with ones that raise when called without an argument, every method of the class named by raise_on_every_method, and the class named by raise_unseeded when constructed without a seed or with None, and that class's seed method when called on an instance without a seed or with None (A03 rule 4: an explicitly seeded instance draws no entropy and stays usable); and install an audit hook that raises on socket, subprocess and ctypes use, on opening any path outside the exchange directory and the readable_paths, and on a fresh import of any module those lists name.
judgement.why: The later note makes the covered set every module named by any of the supplied trap lists, rather than only the newly appended State 2 paths.

topics.topic: Exact stat-result timestamp fields that must be zeroed
questions: Which members of stat_result and DirEntry.stat results must be zeroed, including st_atime, st_mtime, st_ctime and their *_ns forms?
Which fields of `stat_result` and `DirEntry.stat()` must be zeroed, including second and nanosecond forms and any platform-provided creation-time fields?

quotes: It MUST wrap each function named in zero_timestamps so that the stat result it gives, or the entry os.scandir yields gives, carries zero access, modification and change times in seconds and nanoseconds for a descriptor and for every path not under the readable_paths, judged on the path as given, without resolving a link.
judgement.why: The later note explicitly selects access, modification and change times in both seconds and nanoseconds.

topics.topic: Event that counts as a fresh import, including transitive imports
questions: What exact event counts as a fresh import: any import-system load after the name is absent from `sys.modules`, only a direct import statement by the implementation, or also a transitive import performed by another standard-library module?

quotes: runner_source: [BEHAVIOR] The program MUST, before it loads the code, import every module its lists name and only then replace every entry point named in raise_on_call with one that raises whatever arguments it is called with, those in raise_without_argument with ones that raise when called without an argument, every method of the class named by raise_on_every_method, and the class named by raise_unseeded when constructed without a seed or with None, and that class's seed method when called on an instance without a seed or with None (A03 rule 4: an explicitly seeded instance draws no entropy and stays usable); and install an audit hook that raises on socket, subprocess and ctypes use, on opening any path outside the exchange directory and the readable_paths, and on a fresh import of any module those lists name.
judgement.why: The later note applies to any fresh import of a listed module and does not restrict the trap to imports directly initiated by implementation syntax.

topics.topic: Location and runtime classification of the cabinet_sandbox_code file
questions: Where is `cabinet_sandbox_code` stored or mounted, and is its `__file__` always classified outside the read-only runtime so that its timestamps must be zero?

quotes: execute_function: [BEHAVIOR] MUST write into the exchange directory the runner_source text, the code, and every input — a value port's canonical JSON, a file port's bytes, a many file port one file per element in list order — and start the interpreter on the runner file: the command bubblewrap runs is the resolved interpreter path, then the runner file's path inside the environment — runner.py in the exchange directory, /exchange/runner.py —, then the two runner_arguments, in that order, of a RunnerLaunch naming those files by their paths inside the environment, the output ports, the bounds and the channel's descriptor number;
judgement.why: The later note places the implementation code in the exchange directory, outside the read-only runtime and therefore on the zero-timestamp side of the rule.

topics.topic: Source and immutability guarantees for retained runtime-file timestamps
questions: What exact timestamp values belong to a release, where are they recorded, and what guarantees that two installations and later starts of the same release expose the same immutable values rather than build, extraction or host-modification times?

quotes:
The runtime is one Python interpreter with its standard library and nothing
   else, fixed by the kernel release (State 0 questions 4 and 17: photo processing
   is the agent's own work outside the kernel), started with a fixed
   hash seed (`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`) so that set and dict ordering repeats. Adding a
   library is a new kernel release.

A file's
   timestamps read through `os.stat`, `os.lstat`, `os.fstat`, `os.scandir` and their
   `posix` namesakes are zero for a descriptor and for every path not under the
   read-only runtime, judged on the path as the code gives it, without resolving a
   link; a file of the runtime keeps the timestamps its release installed, which
   are no clock because they never change.
judgement.divergence: One release construction preserves installation or host filesystem timestamps, while another normalizes runtime timestamps to release-fixed values; owners or agents comparing equal executions across installations observe different versus equal output digests.
judgement.why: The texts say runtime timestamps belong to the release and never change but do not specify their values, their recorded source, or how equal values are guaranteed across installations of that release.

witness.initial: Two installations run the same kernel release, but their runtime trees were installed or extracted at different times.
events: An agent runs the same implementation with the same input in each installation; the implementation returns the modification timestamp of `os.__file__`.
outcomes: An implementation preserving each runtime tree's filesystem metadata returns different timestamps and output digests across the installations.
An implementation normalizing runtime metadata to release-fixed timestamps returns the same timestamp and output digest in both installations.
witness.observer: The owner or agent comparing the two trial or run outputs.
basis:
The runtime is one Python interpreter with its standard library and nothing
   else, fixed by the kernel release (State 0 questions 4 and 17: photo processing
   is the agent's own work outside the kernel), started with a fixed
   hash seed (`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`) so that set and dict ordering repeats. Adding a
   library is a new kernel release.

A file's
   timestamps read through `os.stat`, `os.lstat`, `os.fstat`, `os.scandir` and their
   `posix` namesakes are zero for a descriptor and for every path not under the
   read-only runtime, judged on the path as the code gives it, without resolving a
   link; a file of the runtime keeps the timestamps its release installed, which
   are no clock because they never change.

An installation selects one manifest instance per service; no flow, run or agent
chooses another. Effectful flows are rehearsed on an installation of disposable
rigs: the owner runs a second kernel installation whose services select their
`disposable_rig` instances, and runs the flow there as anywhere else.

topics.topic: Whether AdmissionVerdict must be regenerated after the A03 sandbox change
questions: After upgrading to this release, may an AdmissionVerdict produced under the former A03 rules still admit and activate an implementation, or must admission run again under the changed sandbox rules?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question as P3 about reuse of an existing admission verdict after the sandbox release change.

precedent.topic: Whether admission must be rerun after the sandbox rule release change
quotes:
Submitting an implementation — new, or equal to an existing one — runs
   admission unless an AdmissionVerdict M08 for that implementation and the
   current corpus digest already exists, in which case that verdict is used.

No issued contract version, implementation, trial case, flow version, value,
   verdict, activation or trace record is edited or deleted by any operation.

The run pins the flow version and, for every function node, the implementation
   of the current activation at start (M19). Nothing recorded later — a new
   activation, a new flow activation, a new binding — changes what the run
   executes.
precedent.why: The texts require reuse of an existing verdict for the same implementation and corpus, preserve existing verdict and activation records, and make a new run pin the implementation currently activated; they specify no loader-change invalidation or readmission.

topics.topic: Whether the sandbox must provide a private /proc or omit /proc
questions: Must the sandbox mount a private proc filesystem so /proc exists, or must /proc be absent under the closed environment described by rule 1?

quotes: execute_function: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST start bubblewrap with new user, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces and no network interface but the new namespace's own loopback, which bubblewrap brings up, with no capability option, the environment cleared and then set exactly to the imported SANDBOX_ENVIRONMENT constant, exactly the host paths of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant bound read-only, inside the new root the symbolic links of the imported SANDBOX_ROOT_SYMLINKS constant (each name linking to its target, made by bubblewrap --symlink), one fresh private exchange directory bound read-write, bubblewrap's own fresh proc mounted at the imported SANDBOX_PROC_MOUNT constant and minimal dev mounts, and no other host directory; the child dies with its parent, and the runner is the init of the new PID namespace (bubblewrap --as-pid-1), so bubblewrap exits only after the host kernel has killed and reaped every other process of that namespace.

The place is now `SANDBOX_PROC_MOUNT` in the data provider
    (`/proc`): `execute_function` mounts the proc there, `runner_arguments`
    passes it as the member `proc_directory`, and the runner lists it.
judgement.why: The later texts require bubblewrap's fresh private proc filesystem to be mounted at `/proc`.
